property_summary: For any caller who is the Owner and any prior balance of the contract, calling withdraw transfers the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0 and c.Owner() still equals the original owner); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can leave funds not sent to Owner (specifically Owner()!=msg.sender) causing address(c).balance or Owner's balance behavior to differ.

For any caller X who is the contract Owner and any contract balance prior to withdraw, after Owner calls withdraw the contract's balance becomes zero (all funds are transferred to Owner); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead can leave the contract balance non-zero when Owner != msg.sender, so the property is violated for some inputs.

For every caller that is the Owner and for every pre-existing contract balance plus any value sent with withdraw, after Owner calls withdraw the Owner address must receive the contract's funds (so Owner's balance increases by the contract balance and address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can break this when Owner != msg.sender by sending funds to a different address, so comparing Owner's balance change versus address(c).balance distinguishes them.

For every call to withdraw made by the contract Owner, the contract's balance becomes zero afterwards (reference always sends all funds to Owner); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender can leave a non-zero contract balance when Owner!=msg.sender, so address(c).balance==0 for all owner withdraws is the property broken by the mutant for some fuzzed owner/caller/address choices.

For any caller who is the contract Owner, after calling withdraw the Owner address retains ownership and the contract balance is zero (i.e., the Owner receives all funds); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can leave the contract with non-zero balance when Owner != msg.sender and thus violates this.

Rule: withdraw always forwards all contract balance to Owner (contract balance becomes zero) when Owner calls it; the mutant using send can fail silently when the Owner's fallback/receive reverts, leaving a non-zero contract balance.

For any caller and any contract balance, when Owner calls withdraw the contract balance becomes zero (reference); the mutant using send can fail to transfer funds if Owner's receiving fallback reverts or runs out of gas, leaving a non-zero contract balance.

For any adversarial recipient contract and any nonzero contract balance, when Owner calls withdraw the reference contract always makes address(c).balance == 0 afterwards (the transfer reverts on failure), whereas the mutant using send can leave a nonzero balance if the Owner's receive/fallback reverts or runs out of gas.

For any owner and any incoming contract balance, when the Owner calls withdraw the reference contract either succeeds and forwards the entire balance to Owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0) or reverts; the mutant using send can silently fail to forward funds and leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs (when Owner's receive/fallback reverts).

For any caller-supplied deposit and any Owner fallback behavior, when the Owner invokes withdraw the reference contract either forwards the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance == 0) or reverts; the mutant that uses send can silently fail to forward funds when Owner's fallback reverts, leaving address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs.
After Command(...) returns, either the call succeeded or the target contract received no Ether (i.e., value forwarded was zero).
Calling Command may revert only if the low-level call would revert when forwarded value is nonzero; specifically, when Command is invoked with zero value it must not revert.
If Command is invoked with nonzero msg.value then the external call it makes may fail; therefore Command never reverts (i.e., reverted==false) whenever msg.value==0.
If the caller is the Owner, calling Command never reverts (original forwards the low-level call without requiring success), so for Owner callers reverted must be false.
When the caller is Owner, Command should not revert (i.e., invoking Command as Owner must succeed).
Command forwards any nonzero msg.value to the target so that calling Command with value>0 changes the target-reachable balance (address(c).balance decreases by that amount).
If the caller is the Owner, then calling Command with any nonzero wei must succeed (not revert).
If amount > 0 then the call to c.Command{value: amount}(adr, data) must not revert (i.e., the Owner can call Command with any msg.value and it will not revert).
If amount > 0 then the call to c.Command{value: amount}(adr, data) does not revert on the original contract (i.e., Owner can call Command with any msg.value and it will not revert).
If amount > 0 then calling c.Command with value amount should not revert (mutant that adds require(msg.value == 0) would cause a revert when amount > 0).
Calling Command with nonzero value does not transfer contract balance away when invoked by the owner (i.e., owner-invoked Command cannot change c's balance).

property_summary: Calls to Command originating from the contract owner always revert (i.e., cannot succeed).
Calls to Command from the contract owner always revert (so reverted == true when msg.sender is Owner).
If the caller equals c.Owner() then calling Command should revert (i.e., (msg.sender == c.Owner()) == reverted).
If this contract's call-site sender equals c.Owner(), then calling Command reverts (i.e., (msg.sender == c.Owner()) == reverted).

For any caller and any calldata, when the Owner calls Command forwarding some ETH, the reference contract forwards the same msg.value to the callee (so the callee receives the ETH), while the mutant that removed the value forwarding will NOT forward ETH and thus the callee's payable fallback/receive won't receive that value (the rule: Owner-called Command forwards msg.value to target).

For any caller and calldata, when the owner invokes Command with some Ether, the reference contract forwards the call as a stateful/value-carrying call to the target (so the low-level call succeeds as a non-static call and target can receive value), while the mutant uses staticcall with no value forwarding which will revert or behave differently for targets that require non-static or payable behavior — thus the reference always allows a payable/stateful invocation to a helper that accepts value, whereas the mutant cannot perform such an invocation for some inputs (fuzzer will find a scenario where the mutant fails).
